erator method is not
callable" at PreferencesScreen.tsx:63; in a RELEASE build a render throw is not
a red box, it is a blank screen with no recovery (Phase-2 finding B-10, P0).

Root cause, traced to the handler rather than guessed: the endpoint answers
`{ data: { preferences: [...], quiet_hours: {...} } }` (aws
src/endpoints/common/me-notifications/src/handlers/preferences.ts — its
`successResponse({ data: { preferences, quiet_hours } })` return), but
`PreferencesResponse` declared `data: PreferenceRow[]` — one level too shallow
AND under the wrong key. So `(await fetchPreferences()).data` handed the screen
an OBJECT, `?? []` never fired because the value is non-null, and `for…of`
threw.

Fixed at the network boundary, not at the `for…of`: `fetchPreferences` now
returns `PreferenceRow[]`, extracting the rows from the canonical envelope and
tolerating two alternates, so a screen never has to know which shape the server
chose. An unrecognised body yields `[]`, which renders as "everything enabled"
— the backend's own semantics for a missing row — instead of throwing. The type
now describes the real wire shape, and the screen keeps one `Array.isArray`
guard: a non-array there is a blank release screen, never a price worth paying
for one predicate.

Fixed at the network boundary, not at the `for…of`: `fetchPreferences` now
returns `PreferenceRow[]`, extracting the rows from the canonical envelope and
tolerating two alternates, so a screen never has to know which shape the server
chose. An unrecognised body yields `[]`, which renders as "everything enabled"

now describes the real wire shape, and the screen keeps one `Array.isArray`
guard: a non-array there is a blank release screen, never a price worth paying
for one predicate.

rulings.what: P1-a (hosted-UI OAuth scope) is REFUTED for the mobile app and needs no fix. The review claimed getUser 401s for Google/Apple customers because hosted-UI tokens cannot carry aws.cognito.signin.user.admin. Verified against source: both apple-oauth.ts and google-oauth.ts mint the tokens they hand the client via ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD_AUTH (apple-oauth.ts:490,575,769,845; google-oauth.ts:716,811), not the hosted-UI /oauth2/token exchange. Cognito API auth flows issue the admin scope, so getUser works.
rulings.why: A release blocker that is not real would have stalled 2.1.0 for nothing; the claim was checkable in one grep and the source contradicts it.
rulings.costIfWrong: If some untraced path DOES return a hosted-UI token to the mobile client, those users 401 on the route and the customer-app client silently refresh-retries the deletion body until it force-logs-out.

rulings.what: P1-b (isOAuthUser is dead) is CONFIRMED and is the real Apple 2.1.0 release blocker, and I am NOT fixing it in this phase. Native Apple/Google accounts are created by adminCreateUser with username=email, custom:role set, and a RANDOM permanent password via adminSetUserPassword (apple-oauth.ts:443-468) - they carry no 'identities' attribute, so isOAuthUser is false and the route demands a password the user was never told. They cannot delete their account.
rulings.why: A correct fix needs a trustworthy signal for 'this account has no user-known password', and the backend has none: user_mgmt.identities has no provider column (cognito_sub, primary_email, timestamps only), commerce.customers has none, and adding a Cognito custom: attribute is forbidden by aws-change-control. The one attribute that correlates - custom:role, set by the OAuth paths and deliberately unset by password signups - attests WHICH ROLE the account is, not whether it has a known password. Inferring the latter from it is the exact error class that produced both P0s in this phase (the URL path, then cognito:groups): using an attribute as evidence for something it does not attest. I will not make it a third time unattended.
rulings.costIfWrong: 2.1.0 ships without a working deletion path for Sign in with Apple users, which is precisely the population guideline 5.1.1(v) is about, and App Review rejects it.

rulings.what: P1-c (the erasure leaves identities.primary_email, device_tokens, web_push_subscriptions and crm.contacts behind while the response says 'Your account has been deleted') is confirmed and deferred. Not fixed here.
rulings.why: Completing it is a DB-content change across four schemas plus a decision about what 'deleted' promises, and the safe form is constrained: identities.primary_email must be scrubbed IN PLACE because hetzner/shim/jit/index.ts gates JIT on identities.cognito_sub - deleting the row re-opens JIT and cognito-post-confirmation's upsert writes the PII back. That is a designed change with its own migration rail, not a tail fix on a deploy.
rulings.costIfWrong: A customer who deletes their account remains re-identifiable by a one-join lookup on an indexed real email, and keeps a live push channel to their handset.

rulings.what: STOPPING code changes to delete-account.ts. The independent review of my own #174 fix found FOUR regressions I introduced in that single unattended pass: (1) the INCORRECT_PASSWORD 400 at :199 is thrown inside the catch I added and rewritten to a 500; (2) my sanitizer collapsed lib/cognito.ts's 14 curated 4xx mappings into that same 500, so a RESET_REQUIRED customer can never delete; (3) my double-tap branch matches UserNotFoundException, which the token-authorized DeleteUser does not return (th
rulings.why: Four defects from one unattended fix to a security-critical route is the signal to stop, not to patch again. The review's own recommended fixes are architectural and far outside this phase: port the intentionality gate into auth-proxy's lib/utils.ts (fixes 17 other routes), make the shim's invoke-emulator noop() set FunctionError (fixes ~40 call sites), and stop the pre-token trigger minting cognito:groups from the requesting client (fixes 27 grant sites, including the admin fleet's only authorization check). Nothing is deployed - the pin is unmerged - so leaving the regressions costs nothing operationally, while a third unattended pass risks a fifth defect.
rulings.costIfWrong: The aws main branch carries a delete-account route with four known defects until someone fixes them; anyone who merges the pin without reading the handoff ships them to production.

This is Phase 7's stale-bundle lesson in a new costume: a negative result measured through a too-fast probe.

rulings.what: Did NOT apply D1's material=solid escape hatch to /sessions or /marketplace/all-robots
rulings.why: The plan says switch 'if it hitches'. Measured from the Maestro recordings: both lists hold a MEDIAN 15.0ms frame gap (~66fps). /sessions has the worse tail (p95 46.7ms, 72/595 gaps >33ms = 12.1%) vs all-robots (p95 20.0ms, 27/1232 = 2.2%), but neither sustains a stall — the >500ms outliers are the idle periods between swipes. A simulator VFR capture is not a device performance measurement, so degrading the material on this evidence would trade a documented look for an unproven gain.
rulings.costIfWrong: If the lists DO hitch on real hardware, /sessions is the one to switch first; the recordings + numbers are in reports/phase-08 so the next session need not re-measure.

rulings.what: Built, layout-verified and then REVERTED the /sign-in keyboard-avoidance fix (removing the nested FormWrapper); left it for a device/working-keyboard pass
rulings.why: P6 assigned this fix to Phase 8 and the root cause is written down: sign-in-screen.tsx wraps SchemaForm in a FormWrapper and SchemaForm mounts a second one — on native a FormWrapper IS a KeyboardAwareScrollView, so two nest and the inner content-height one has nothing to scroll. The edit typechecked and the screen rendered identically. But the simulator would NOT raise a software keyboard even with ConnectHardwareKeyboard=0 and a full Simulator restart (r2's stated precondition), so the flow passed VACUOUSLY — the exact vacuous-pass trap that report warns about.
